name: What is firewalld?
description:
Introduction to firewalld

firewalld is the default firewall management tool on CentOS 7+ and Fedora. It provides a dynamic firewall with support for network zones.

Check if firewalld is running:

$ systemctl status firewalld

If it's not running, start it:

$ systemctl start firewalld

The main command-line tool is firewall-cmd. Check the state:

$ firewall-cmd --state

It should say running.

name: Understanding Zones
description:
Firewall Zones

firewalld uses zones to define the level of trust for network connections. Each zone has rules about what traffic is allowed.

Common zones:

ZonePurpose
publicDefault zone — untrusted networks
homeHome network — some trust
trustedAll traffic allowed
dropAll incoming dropped silently
blockAll incoming rejected with ICMP message

List all available zones:

$ firewall-cmd --get-zones

Check the default zone:

$ firewall-cmd --get-default-zone

See the active zone and interfaces:

$ firewall-cmd --get-active-zones

name: Allowing Services
description:
Opening Ports for Services

The most common task — allow a service through the firewall.

See what's currently allowed:

$ firewall-cmd --list-all

Allow HTTP (port 80):

$ firewall-cmd --add-service=http

Allow HTTPS (port 443):

$ firewall-cmd --add-service=https

Verify:

$ firewall-cmd --list-services

You should see http and https in the list.

Important: These changes are temporary — they disappear after a restart. To make them permanent, add --permanent:

$ firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service=http
$ firewall-cmd --reload
answer: Always use --permanent for changes you want to survive a reboot, then --reload to apply them.

name: Opening Specific Ports
description:
Custom Port Numbers

Sometimes you need to open a specific port that doesn't match a named service.

Open port 8080 for TCP:

$ firewall-cmd --permanent --add-port=8080/tcp

Open a range of ports:

$ firewall-cmd --permanent --add-port=5000-5100/tcp

Open a UDP port:

$ firewall-cmd --permanent --add-port=53/udp

Apply changes:

$ firewall-cmd --reload

List all open ports:

$ firewall-cmd --list-ports

Remove a port:

$ firewall-cmd --permanent --remove-port=8080/tcp
$ firewall-cmd --reload

name: Rich Rules
description:
Advanced Rules

Rich rules give you more control — allow/deny specific IPs, logging, etc.

Allow SSH only from a specific IP:

$ firewall-cmd --permanent --add-rich-rule='rule family=ipv4 source address=192.168.1.100 service name=ssh accept'

Block all traffic from an IP:

$ firewall-cmd --permanent --add-rich-rule='rule family=ipv4 source address=10.0.0.50 drop'

Log and allow HTTP from a subnet:

$ firewall-cmd --permanent --add-rich-rule='rule family=ipv4 source address=192.168.1.0/24 service name=http log prefix="HTTP" level="info" accept'

List all rich rules:

$ firewall-cmd --list-rich-rules

Don't forget to reload:

$ firewall-cmd --reload

name: Changing Zones
description:
Working with Zones

Change the default zone:

$ firewall-cmd --set-default-zone=home

See all settings for a specific zone:

$ firewall-cmd --zone=home --list-all

Add a service to a specific zone (not just the default):

$ firewall-cmd --zone=home --permanent --add-service=samba

Move an interface to a different zone:

$ firewall-cmd --zone=trusted --change-interface=eth0

Check which zone an interface belongs to:

$ firewall-cmd --get-zone-of-interface=eth0

Set it back to public:

$ firewall-cmd --set-default-zone=public

name: Panic Mode and Troubleshooting
description:
Emergency and Debugging

If you suspect your server is under attack, enable panic mode — drops ALL network traffic:

$ firewall-cmd --panic-on

Turn it off:

$ firewall-cmd --panic-off

Check if panic mode is active:

$ firewall-cmd --query-panic

Troubleshooting tips:

See the full runtime config vs permanent config:

$ firewall-cmd --list-all          # runtime
$ firewall-cmd --list-all --permanent  # permanent

If they differ, you forgot to --reload after making permanent changes.

Check firewalld logs:

$ journalctl -u firewalld
answer: Never use panic mode on a remote server unless you have physical/console access — you'll lock yourself out!
